top_news.title: Mease, Howell vie for Haywood sheriff -
top_news.summary: Haywood County will have a new sheriff for the second time this decade. Mark Mease, a Republican, and Tyler Howell, a Democrat, are Haywood County natives whose families go back generations in Western North Carolina. Both men have also worked full-time law enforcement jobs while campaigning. Perhaps the most striking similarity is that both prefer to shun the political angling required during a campaign — at least during the General Election — saying they would prefer if the office of sheriff wasn’t even partisan. The candidates, who’ve pledged to each other and voters to refrain from mudslinging during the General Election campaign, are instead trying to run on their merits and ideas. The winner will replace current Sheriff Bill Wilke. Here’s a look at what they said during their interviews with The Smoky Mountain News.

top_news.title: Copper landline customers will keep service for now: Will broadband expand fast enough to keep WNC connected? -
top_news.summary: As telecommunication giants accelerate the nationwide phaseout of legacy copper phone lines, several Western North Carolina residents are receiving notice that the landlines they have relied on for decades are nearing retirement. Nantahala resident Susan Carpenter got one of these letters from her phone company, Verizon, and at a September Macon County Commissioners meeting, asked, “What is the plan?” For households tucked into the region’s hollers and dead zones, many, like Carpenter, worry the transition threatens to sever their primary connection to emergency services and the outside world. In an interview with The Smoky Mountain News, Verizon spokesperson Lauren Peterson emphasized that copper customers will not be stranded without a fallback.

articles.title: Mease, Howell vie for Haywood sheriff -
articles.summary: Haywood County will have a new sheriff for the second time this decade. Mark Mease, a Republican, and Tyler Howell, a Democrat, are Haywood County natives whose families go back generations in Western North Carolina. Both men have also worked full-time law enforcement jobs while campaigning. Perhaps the most striking similarity is that both prefer to shun the political angling required during a campaign — at least during the General Election — saying they would prefer if the office of sheriff wasn’t even partisan. The candidates, who’ve pledged to each other and voters to refrain from mudslinging during the General Election campaign, are instead trying to run on their merits and ideas. The winner will replace current Sheriff Bill Wilke. Here’s a look at what they said during their interviews with The Smoky Mountain News.
